title: Hollywood
name: Hollywood
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for Hollywood soundstage and production-support real estate, Hollywood Boulevard retail, and multifamily near the studio district.

sections.html: Hollywood runs on production as much as on tourism, and an exchange buyer identifying property here is choosing between studio-support real estate, tourist-corridor retail, and a wave of new multifamily towers that has grown up around both. The three markets sit blocks apart from each other but do not behave the same way, and a rent roll drawn from one tells a buyer very little about the other two.

sections.heading: Soundstages and Production-Support Space
sections.html:
Long-established studio lots and independent soundstage facilities around Sunset and Gower still anchor a meaningful production-support real estate market in Hollywood, including sound mixing, editorial, and equipment-rental space that leases to production companies on shorter, activity-driven terms than a standard office tenant. A buyer replacing into this niche should underwrite occupancy against production-cycle volatility rather than assuming the steady renewal pattern typical of a professional office tenant.

Several of these facilities also carry specialized soundproofing, power capacity, and loading-dock configurations installed for a specific production tenant's equipment, and a buyer should confirm what portion of that build-out would transfer to a different production tenant versus what is essentially sunk cost tied to the current occupant. Vacancy in this niche can sit unfilled longer than a standard office suite precisely because the pool of tenants able to use a purpose-built soundstage is smaller than the pool of tenants who can use generic office space.

sections.heading: Hollywood Boulevard Retail's Tourism Dependence
sections.html: Retail along Hollywood Boulevard and the Walk of Fame draws almost entirely from tourist foot traffic rather than a local resident base, and that dependence showed clearly during the pandemic-era travel slowdown when vacancy on the boulevard rose sharply. A rent roll here should be reviewed against pre-pandemic tourism volumes as a baseline rather than the most recent twelve months alone, since recovery has not been uniform block by block, and it has generally lagged the broader Los Angeles retail market's recovery pace.

sections.heading: New Multifamily Around the Studios
sections.html:
Hollywood has added a meaningful amount of new high-rise and mid-rise multifamily over the past decade, much of it built to serve production workers and younger renters who want to live near the studios and Sunset Strip nightlife. These newer buildings sit outside the city's older rent stabilization coverage, unlike much of the pre-1978 apartment stock nearby, which makes them a materially different underwriting case than an older Hollywood courtyard building on the same block.

Amenity packages on these newer towers, rooftop pools, coworking lounges, and package-handling systems in particular, have become a real competitive factor in lease-up speed, and a replacement buyer should weigh ongoing amenity operating costs against the rent premium those features command before assuming the premium is pure profit. A building that opened its amenity floor several years ago may also be due for a refresh cycle sooner than a buyer coming from an older, amenity-light submarket would expect.

sections.heading: What a Hollywood Identification Usually Includes
sections.html:
A realistic Hollywood list draws from:

  • soundstage and production-support buildings near Sunset and Gower
  • Hollywood Boulevard and Vine Street retail storefronts
  • newer market-rate apartment towers built within the last decade
  • older courtyard and dingbat-style apartment buildings covered by rent stabilization

sections.heading: Rent Stabilization Splits the Multifamily Bench
sections.html:
Because Hollywood's apartment stock spans everything from 1920s courtyard buildings to brand-new towers, a multifamily identification here has to specify which side of that split the target property falls on before a rent roll means anything. Confirming construction date and stabilization status early, ideally before the property goes on the identification list, keeps a buyer from discovering a covered-unit surprise deep into the 45-day window.

A lender underwriting an older, stabilization-covered Hollywood building will also want to see a unit-by-unit history of rent increases and any pending habitability complaints, since a building with deferred maintenance on a rent-stabilized rent roll carries a different risk profile than the same deferred maintenance on a market-rate building where rents can reset faster after a renovation.

faqs.q: Is Hollywood retail a stable 1031 replacement option compared to other Los Angeles retail corridors?
faqs.a: It can be, but Hollywood Boulevard retail depends heavily on tourism volume, so a buyer should weigh recovery trends over several years rather than relying on a single recent quarter of foot traffic and sales data, and should compare that recovery pace against other Los Angeles retail corridors before assuming Hollywood is representative.

faqs.q: What makes soundstage and production-support real estate different to underwrite?
faqs.a: Tenants in this niche tend to lease on shorter, activity-driven terms tied to production schedules, so occupancy can move with the entertainment industry's production cycle rather than following typical office renewal patterns.

faqs.q: Are new Hollywood apartment towers covered by the same rent stabilization rules as older buildings?
faqs.a: Generally not. Most of the recent high-rise and mid-rise construction falls outside the city's older rent stabilization coverage, unlike much of the pre-1978 courtyard and dingbat-style stock nearby, and a buyer should confirm a specific building's status rather than assume either way.

faqs.q: How does Hollywood compare to Burbank for production-related real estate?
faqs.a: Hollywood offers older, smaller-scale soundstage and support space closer to legacy studio lots, while Burbank's studio campuses and surrounding industrial space tend to be larger and more corporate in scale, which changes both the tenant pool and the typical lease term a buyer should expect.

faqs.q: What diligence matters most for an older Hollywood apartment building?
faqs.a: Confirm rent stabilization coverage and any pending habitability or code issues tied to the building's age, since older courtyard-style buildings in this submarket carry a different compliance history than the newer towers built nearby, and any open code case should be resolved or clearly priced into the deal before closing.
